title: From Text to Your First Python Code
why_this_order: Prerequisite-driven learning while retaining reconstructed Git history and cross-file links; not one commit per lesson.

text: We are going to build a real project called nanoGPT. It learns patterns in text and can generate new text.
You are starting from zero. We'll begin with tiny Python programs, and every step will connect back to the same project.
slides.title: Build nanoGPT from zero

text: Imagine the computer sees the letters hel. A text generator might predict that the next letter is l.
Later we will see how the real nanoGPT model learns to make predictions. Today we start with understanding text.
The whole project follows one journey. We prepare text, build a model, train it, then use it to generate text.
These are connected parts of one application—not separate exercises.
Python is a programming language. We write instructions that a computer can follow.
A Python source file usually ends in .py.
print(...) tells Python to display something.
The words inside quotes are text.
What will this program display?
slides.why: The text between quotes is AI. print() displays it.

text: In Python, "hello" is called a string. A string means text.
Quotes tell Python to treat the characters as text.
We can store text under a name instead of typing it again and again.
This named storage is called a variable.
In text = "hello", the name is text and its stored value is hello.
The sign = assigns a value to a name.
Which part is the variable name?
slides.why: text is the variable name; "hello" is its value.

text: When we write print(text) without quotes around text, Python prints the stored value.
print(text) and print("text") are different.
The first uses the variable. The second prints the literal word text.
What will these statements print?
slides.why: The variable contains cat, but the quoted text is the word word.

text: Let's use the same small piece of text through the next steps.
It contains five characters, including a space.
A character can be a letter, punctuation, or a space.
"to be" contains t, o, a space, b and e.
Python has a function called len().
It counts how many characters are in a string.
What will this display?
slides.why: A, I, and ! make three characters.

text: A character's position is called an index.
In Python the first character has index 0, not 1.
text[0] means the first character of text.
text[1] means the second character because counting starts from zero.
What is at index 2?
slides.why: Index 2 is the space between the words. Spaces count as characters.

text: You can now read these four lines as one program.
It stores text, displays it, counts its characters and finds the first one.
Predict the output, in order.
slides.why: Index 0 is d, and dog contains three characters.

slides.tag: WHERE IS THIS IN THE REAL PROJECT?
text: The project needs far more than "to be". It uses a file containing Shakespeare's text.
The real script data/shakespeare_char/prepare.py reads that text before preparing it for the model.
The repository contains this exact line. It stores the text read from a file in a variable named data.
We haven't learned with, open, or file reading yet. We'll return to those details later.
The next real line prints the length of the dataset.
You already know part of this: len(data) counts the characters stored in data.
An f-string lets Python insert a calculated value into text.
The part inside {...} is evaluated and inserted into the message.
What does this print?
slides.why: The string hello has five characters, so the f-string inserts 5.

text: In the real source, :, asks Python to put commas between thousands.
It changes how the number looks, not what the number means.
print displays text, f inserts a value, len(data) counts characters, and :, formats the number.
This is the real project's data-length output.
Why does the original script use len(data)?
slides.why: len(data) counts how many characters were loaded.

text: Next the script will find which unique characters exist in the book.
Here is the real next-stage expression. Don't memorize set, list or sorted yet. They belong in Chapter 2.
prepare.py prepares the text. train.py uses it to train a GPT defined in model.py.
sample.py then uses the trained model to generate new text.
The reconstructed Git history begins with a model header, imports, and LayerNorm code.
We are deliberately learning text and Python first, because understanding the eventual model requires these foundations.
We'll return to those early model commits when you know enough to understand them.
Which file is responsible for preparing the small character-level Shakespeare dataset?
slides.why: The Shakespeare character-level preparation script loads text and prepares it for training.

text: What happens when this code tries to access index 3?
slides.why: The only valid nonnegative indices are 0, 1 and 2.

text: Write a tiny Python program that stores "hello" in a variable named text.
Then print its length and its first character.
The in-page checker only inspects your text. Run it in Python and share the output if you want independent verification.
You can now recognize a Python string, variable, print(), len(), indexing and a simple f-string.
You also understand what the dataset-length line does in the real project. We have not claimed mastery of file reading, tokenization or PyTorch.
